title: The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order
gist: Kupchan argues globalization has peaked and the world is fragmenting into regional blocs — a third of U.S. trade with Canada and Mexico, two-thirds of EU trade internal, over half of Asian commerce intra-regional — and proposes a permanent, continuously sitting Global Concert of China, the EU, India, Japan, Russia and the U.S. plus regional-body emissaries, headquartered in Istanbul or Dubai, to supply the top-down coordination the veto-paralyzed U.N. cannot.

insights.claim: Globalization has peaked and trade is already regionalizing hard: almost one-third of U.S. trade is with Canada and Mexico, roughly two-thirds of EU trade is intra-bloc, and intra-regional trade exceeds half of Asia's international commerce.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Regional trade intensity is the baseline, not a forecast — position for continued outperformance of regional logistics, near-shore manufacturing and intra-bloc supply chains over long-haul global routes.
insights.quote: Almost one-third of U.S. trade is with Canada and Mexico, some two-thirds of European Union trade takes place within the bloc, and intra-regional trade makes up more than half of Asia’s international commerce.
insights.locator: The same goes for trade

insights.claim: Tariffs, friendshoring, supply-chain repatriation and other forms of economic decoupling are poised to deepen the regional trade concentration further, making regions the primary sites of commercial activity.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: The fragmentation trade has a long runway; capex in regional duplicate capacity is a multi-year theme rather than a policy-cycle blip.
insights.quote: Regions are becoming increasingly important sites of commercial activity.
insights.locator: These trends are poised to deepen due to tariffs

insights.claim: Canada, alienated by Trump's America First policies, is seeking a new home among middle powers but will remain deeply integrated into North America both strategically and commercially regardless of political alienation.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Canadian diversification rhetoric will not materially reduce U.S. trade dependence — fade headlines about Canada pivoting away from the U.S. market.
insights.quote: But like it or not, Canada will remain deeply integrated into North America both strategically and commercially.
insights.locator: Canada, alienated by Trump’s America First policies

themes.theme: Polycentric order and legitimized spheres of influence

insights.claim: Power diffusion is structural and unstoppable, so no single country or coalition will dominate: the U.S. and its democratic allies remain formidable but not preponderant, and China will be a peer competitor without the power or appeal to anchor a Sinocentric world order even with Russia.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Neither a U.S.-led restoration nor a China-led replacement is the base case — plan for persistent fragmentation with no hegemonic backstop for global public goods.
insights.quote: This change is structural—a product of the unstoppable diffusion of power.
insights.locator: As the West’s ideological and material hegemony

insights.claim: Automation combined with free trade undermined the industrial-era social contract, hollowing out Western middle classes and the political centrism that sustained liberal internationalism — making the domestic collapse of liberal order a direct consequence of technology and trade.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Ties the AI/automation cycle directly to political instability in developed markets — expect the same mechanism to intensify as AI displaces service work.
insights.quote: A combination of automation and free trade has undermined the industrial-era social contract, hollowing out Western middle classes and the political centrism that sustained liberal internationalism.
insights.locator: As the West’s ideological and material hegemony

insights.claim: Trump is a symptom more than a cause of the disarray, and populists who promise to tear down the liberal order lack the skills and inclination to build a replacement — leaving a governance vacuum that must be filled after he leaves.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: The disorder outlasts the administration; no mean-reversion trade on a post-Trump restoration of the rules-based system.
insights.quote: He and other populists promise to tear down the old liberal order. But they lack the skills and inclination to build what comes next.
insights.locator: U.S. President Donald Trump is a symptom more than a cause

insights.claim: Regionalized governance would to some extent bring back and legitimize spheres of influence, which Kupchan accepts as inevitable in a world of diffusing power while arguing the delegitimation of imperial rule makes consensual influence more likely than coercive.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: A mainstream U.S. scholar conceding spheres of influence signals the direction of Western policy debate — country risk will increasingly be priced by bloc membership.
insights.quote: the regionalization of global governance would to some extent bring back and legitimize spheres of influence. Yet that outcome is inevitable in a world of diffusing power.
insights.locator: By encouraging major powers to hold sway

insights.claim: Russia might be less aggressive toward its neighbors if it believed the U.S. would refrain from extending strategic reach into Russia's rimlands, and Beijing might pursue regional objectives less coercively if U.S.-China rivalry cooled — framing adversary aggression as partly responsive to Western encroachment.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: A live policy argument for negotiated restraint over containment — if it gains traction it would reshape the risk premium on Eastern Europe and Taiwan.
insights.locator: Admittedly, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine

insights.claim: Regional bodies both empower and check their largest members — the EU constrains Germany and France, the GCC both enables and restrains Saudi Arabia, ASEAN does the same for Indonesia, and RCEP binds China to consensual rules despite its economic size.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Regional institutions are a real constraint on hegemonic behavior — RCEP in particular is an underrated brake on Chinese unilateralism in trade.
insights.locator: EU membership may expose less powerful member states

insights.claim: New regional bodies will need to be created in South Asia and Northeast Asia, where capable institutions are absent precisely because geopolitical tensions have arrested regional integration.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: The two regions with the least institutional shock-absorption are also two of the highest-tension flashpoints — a structural argument for higher tail risk in Korea/Japan/China and India/Pakistan.
insights.locator: Some regional bodies, such as the Arab League

insights.claim: The proposed Global Concert would seat China, the EU, India, Japan, Russia and the United States plus emissaries from ASEAN, the Arab League, the African Union and the Organization of American States — with Europe represented by the EU rather than Germany to legitimize regional-body representation.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: A concrete blueprint for post-U.N. great-power coordination worth tracking; adoption would shift where geopolitical decisions actually get made.
insights.locator: The Global Concert would serve as a great-power directorate

insights.claim: The Global Concert would sit continuously and daily rather than as fly-in summits, headquartered in a city between West and East such as Istanbul or Dubai, because G-7, G-20 and BRICS summitry is 'woefully inadequate.'
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: A vote of no confidence in existing summit diplomacy; also a marker of where diplomatic infrastructure and influence could migrate geographically.
insights.quote: Fly-in, fly-out summits, whether of the G-7, the G-20, or BRICS, are woefully inadequate.
insights.locator: As in the Concert of Europe, ideological differences

insights.claim: A subconcert on technology and AI regulation would seat major tech company representatives alongside states, NGOs and universities — formally elevating corporations to participants in international governance.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: AI governance is heading toward a state-plus-industry negotiating format; the largest model providers would gain direct seats at the rule-making table.
insights.quote: The subconcert focused on the regulation of technology and artificial intelligence, for example, could include representatives from the major tech companies
insights.locator: In addition to serving as a high-level steering group

insights.claim: Subconcerts would be established for Ukraine, Israel-Palestine, Iran and Taiwan, plus international commerce, climate, technology, global health and human development — a named list of the flashpoints the author considers most in need of sustained diplomacy.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: A compact list of the four geopolitical situations most likely to produce discontinuous market events over the next decade.
insights.locator: Subconcerts would be established to address geopolitical flashpoints

insights.claim: Concert members would be disarmed of veto power and meet behind closed doors, with the body consultative — teeing up decisions the U.N. and other institutions would finalize — explicitly designed to strengthen rather than sideline the U.N.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: The workaround to Security Council paralysis is procedural, not structural — a lower-cost path to reform than charter amendment, hence more likely to actually happen.
insights.locator: The Global Concert, backstopped by the subconcerts

themes.theme: Informal small-group diplomacy is already the norm

insights.claim: The shift to informal small-group diplomacy is already happening by default — the 1990s Balkans contact group, the P5+1 Iran deal, Oman/Pakistan/Qatar mediating Iran-U.S., Trump's Board of Peace on Gaza, and Egypt/Saudi Arabia/UAE/U.S. on Sudan's civil war.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Watch ad hoc coalitions, not formal institutions, for the signals that actually move conflicts — the list names who currently holds mediation leverage.
insights.quote: Ad hoc groupings and coalitions of the willing have become the new normal.
insights.locator: A contact group of Britain, France, Germany, Italy

insights.claim: Institutionalized multilateralism will become increasingly elusive because populist nationalism intensifies domestic opposition to binding international commitments, and stalemate in the Security Council and WTO is already the norm.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Do not expect binding global rules on trade, tech or climate; governance will arrive as reversible informal understandings, raising policy volatility.
insights.quote: Amid a widespread surge in populist nationalism, institutionalized multilateralism will be increasingly elusive.
insights.locator: These obstacles to institutionalized cooperation

insights.claim: Western democracies should pragmatically welcome BRICS and SCO public-goods delivery — BRICS lending to emerging economies, SCO cooperation against human and weapons trafficking — rather than treating them purely as rival blocs.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: BRICS development lending is real capital flow into emerging markets regardless of the bloc's geopolitical framing — treat it as a funding source, not just a headline.
insights.locator: Collective efforts will be easier to come by

insights.claim: Regional actors closest to a threat have the strongest incentive to counter it — Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have more at stake in containing Iran than the U.S. did even while leading this year's air campaign against Tehran.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: Burden-shifting to regional powers means Gulf states' defense procurement and security commitments rise structurally as U.S. leadership recedes.

insights.claim: Historically, ordering moments follow major wars — Westphalia 1648, the Concert of Europe 1815, the League of Nations 1920, the U.N. 1945 — and the world now needs one before rather than after another great-power war.
insights.speaker: Charles A. Kupchan
insights.so_what: The historical base rate implies order-building typically requires a catastrophe first — a sobering prior on how likely pre-emptive reform actually is.
insights.quote: Ordering moments tend to follow major wars.
insights.locator: Ordering moments tend to follow major wars
